newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU threatens Boeing/McDonnell Douglas deal.
newsitem.headline: EU threatens Boeing/McDonnell Douglas deal.

text.p: The European Union threw down the gauntlet to Boeing and McDonnell Douglas on Friday, saying their planned $14 billion merger should be blocked under EU antitrust law unless it was changed.
EU sources said competition experts from all 15 EU countries had agreed at a meeting in Brussels that offers made to date by Boeing for the deal to pass muster were "not sufficient".
"If adequate remedies are not offered, the proposed concentration should be prohibited," one source said, summing up the experts' conclusions.

Sources said the experts -- an advisory committee -- had unanimously agreed with European Commission competition officials that the merger would add to what was seen as Boeing's already dominant position in the aircraft industry.
"Commitments offered so far by Boeing are not sufficient to prevent such a strengthening of dominant position," another source said.
Boeing was not immediately available for comment.
The sources said the Commission, the EU's antitrust watchdog, planned in the next few days to find out whether Boeing was prepared to come up with further offers to allow the deal to go through.
These would have to address three areas in which the Commission has made its concerns clear.

Firstly, it opposes Boeing's exclusive contracts to supply aircraft to certain airlines, notably Delta, American and Continental, an matter which is viewed by various industry experts as a side issue.
More significant are Commission worries about the possibility of spillovers of public money, earmarked for research and development in defence, into Boeing's civil aviation business.
EU officials are also unhappy about the size of the deal itself.
Commission figures say the merger would give the merged firms a 70 percent share of the market for large civil aircraft -- those with more than 100 seats.
On the point of the deal size, three possible remedies have surfaced for Boeing to secure Commission approval.

These are the sale of McDonnell Douglas's civil aviation manufacturing capacity, the sale, or rather non-purchase by Boeing, of McDonnell's civil aviation businesses and, the third, possibily likeliest one, the sale of McDonnell's licensing, after-sales and support services.

Europe's position is in sharp contrast to that of anti-trust authorities in the United States, where last Tuesday Federal trade commissioners agreed four to one not to challenge any aspect of the deal, saying McDonnell Douglas was no longer a competitive force in the commercial aircraft market.
They did, however, say that Boeing's exclusive contracts were "potentially troubling".
